newsitem.title: GREECE: FARMERS ELUDE GREEK POLICE IN HIDE-AND-SEEK.
newsitem.headline: FARMERS ELUDE GREEK POLICE IN HIDE-AND-SEEK.

text.p: Greek farmers drove their tractors under bridges and through cotton fields to elude police for the second day on Wednesday as Prime Minister Costas Simitis chaired an urgent cabinet meeting to deal with the revolt.
"Our target is to reach the points we have chosen on the national road and block them. We have the upper hand and we proved that we can do it," farmers' representative Yannis Patakis told reporters.
Police units struggled with mud in freezing temperatures all day Tuesday chasing tractors through vast farmlands where a number of police cars got stuck.

The farmers, pressing for cheaper fuel and state subsidies, have vowed to repeat a crippling 25-day blockade of national roads last December but Simitis warned them that if necessary he would use force to keep the roads open this time.
He sent about 5,000 police, many in riot gear, and helicopters to track down the farmers and prevent them from occupying highways with their tractors.
But on Tuesday farmers drove at will their tractors on the main north-south highway and pulled back into the fields when riot police units showed up.
"We will have more hide-and-seek today, but will not clash with the police," Thanassis Nasikas, another farmers' leader said. "The government must and will understand our problems and solve them."
Athens' main newspapers were unanimous on Wednesday that the farmers had won the "first round" with the government and ministers were out of mood and angry as they walked into the cabinet meeting.

"This hide-and-seek game by the farmers is ridiculous and takes us many years back," Agriculture Minister Stephanos Tzoumakas told reporters before the cabinet meeting. "The state can't subsidise products because it's against the law, and that is that."
He accused the Greek Communist Party (KKE) of being behind the revolt and said its political target was to show that the government did not care for workers' problems and was authoritarian.

The farmers' main road block, with more than 1,500 tractors, was outside Drougos village south of Larissa where they occupied an old north-south road. Police said no cars were stranded and that the effect on traffic was minimal.
"We will again avoid clashes today. Highways are open and will stay that way," Public Order Minister George Romeos said.

The farmers gave up the December blockade because of the Christmas holidays but vowed to bring their tractors back to highways if their demands for higher price supports, cheaper fuel and tax cuts were not met.

Simitis, struggling to bring Greece closer to its European Union partners with a tough 1997 budget, has turned down demands by various protesting labour unions saying the state could not afford one extra drachma for any specific group.
